# Data in BiologyToML: everything is generated by code

The repository stores **no data files and no pictures**. Every data set, figure and picture in
the 45 notebooks is produced by code that runs inside the notebook. Data come from the
simulators in [`course_toolkit.py`](course_toolkit.py) (copied verbatim into each notebook that
uses them) or from small simulation functions written in the notebook itself.

Why simulate?

- **A known truth.** Every simulator returns the hidden truth — the true cell types, the true
  network, the causal SNPs, the true mutation effects — so every method can be *checked*: the
  notebooks contain 🧪 *ground-truth checks* that real data could not provide.
- **A slim, self-contained repository.** Nothing to download, no licences to track, no broken
  links; every notebook runs offline on a free CPU in minutes.
- **Reproducible.** Fixed default seeds mean every notebook (and every student) sees the same data
  and the same numbers.

What simulation cannot teach — the messiness of real data — is covered in each Level 2 module's
🧭 *From toy to real data* section, which names the public data sets and production tools to use
next. The synthetic look-alikes reproduce the *structure* of the classic studies (sizes, classes,
typical effect sizes, correlations, detection limits); they never reproduce published numbers,
and the notebooks say so.

---

## Synthetic look-alikes of the classic 02-620 examples (Level 1)

| Simulator | Mimics | What it returns (hidden truth in **bold**) | Modules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `simulate_leukemia_expression()` | Golub *et al.* (1999) leukaemia microarrays: 72 patients (47 ALL — 38 B-lineage, 9 T-lineage — and 25 AML) × 3,571 genes, log10 scale, detection floor 2.0, the original 38/34 training/test design | `X`, `y`, `labels`, **`subtype`**, `genes` (54 named marker genes in `LEUKEMIA_MARKERS`, after the genes that separated the leukaemias in the original study), `is_train`, `sample_id`, **`atypical`** (two weak-signature AML samples), **`true_effect`** | 00–05, 08, 09, 11–14, 22, 23, 44 |
| `simulate_signaling_cytometry(kind)` | Sachs *et al.* (2005) single-cell phospho-protein flow cytometry of human T cells: 11 proteins, unperturbed cells plus targeted interventions; continuous or low/medium/high | `data`, `intervention`, **`edges`** (the 20-edge consensus network the data are generated from), **`weights`** | 15–18, 44 |
| `simulate_prostate_clinical()` | Stamey *et al.* (1989) prostate-cancer study: 97 men, 8 clinical measurements, log PSA, a 67/30 split | the table; `lpsa` is generated from the predictors with the original study's least-squares coefficients (Hastie *et al.* 2009, Table 3.2) | 03, 04, 06, 07, 21, 23 |
| `simulate_tumor_features()` | Wisconsin diagnostic breast-cancer data (Street *et al.* 1993): 569 aspirates, 30 nuclear features (mean/error/worst of 10 properties) | `X`, `y` (1 = malignant), `target_names`; geometric relations and a shared irregularity factor make features strongly correlated | 09, 10, 11, 23 |
| `simulate_blood_cells()` | a three-class flow-cytometry gating problem (lymphocytes, monocytes, granulocytes; FSC, SSC, CD45, CD14) — the course's stand-in for the iris data | `X`, **`y`**, `class_names` | 09, 10 |
| `simulate_cell_images()` | microscopy images of single nuclei (round, elongated, kidney, segmented, dividing, ring) — the stand-in for handwritten digits | `images`, `X`, **`y`**, `class_names` | 14 |
| `simulate_genotypes()`, `simulate_quantitative_trait()` | Hardy–Weinberg genotypes with optional population structure (Balding–Nichols F_ST); polygenic traits with chosen heritability | genotype matrix, **population labels**, **causal SNPs and effects** | 01–03, 05–07, 10, 13, 21, 23, 25, 35, 42, 44 |
| Typed-in worked examples (toolkit) | PlayTennis (Mitchell 1997), a six-person genotype table for naïve Bayes, the burglary/earthquake alarm network, the two-dice HMM | small tables (`PLAY_TENNIS_ROWS`, `NB_GENOTYPE_TABLE`, `ALARM_CPTS`, `DICE_HMM`) | 05, 08, 10, 15–17, 19, 20 |
| Typed-in worked examples (in the notebook) | the classic textbook census table P(wealth, gender, hours) with its eight probabilities; the human preproinsulin coding sequence (333 nt) and its protein (UniProt P01308), typed in as short strings for the genetic-code exercise; a seven-sequence classroom cartoon of a GWAS | literals in the cell that uses them, labelled as typed-in examples (nothing is downloaded) | 00, 02, 05 (census); 01 (insulin); 06 (cartoon) |

## Simulators for the research frontier (Level 2)

| Simulator | Mimics | Hidden truth | Modules |
|---|---|---|---|
| `simulate_scrna(...)` | droplet scRNA-seq UMI counts of blood cells (PBMC-like types with real marker names), donors, batches, interferon stimulation (cf. Kang *et al.* 2018); optional doublets, damaged and cycling cells | cell types, donors, batches, condition, **per-type stimulation effects** (`true_logfc`), marker genes | 24, 25, 27, 29–31, 34, 42–44 |
| `simulate_differentiation(...)` | a time course in which progenitors split into two fates; unspliced and spliced counts from transcription kinetics (du/dt = α − βu, ds/dt = βu − γs) | **latent time, fate, kinetic rates, true velocity** | 32 |
| `simulate_spatial_tissue(...)` | a tumour section at single-cell resolution plus Visium-like spots: tumour core, invasive margin, stroma, epithelium; hypoxia gradient; T-cell exhaustion near tumour cells | **domains, cell types, spot compositions**, the planted spatial programmes | 33 |
| `simulate_multiome(...)` | trimodal single cells: RNA + surface protein (CITE-seq, with isotype background) + chromatin accessibility (ATAC) | cell types and **states visible in only one modality** (naive/memory T cells and Tregs in protein; primed monocytes in ATAC), **peak–gene links** | 34 |
| `simulate_perturb_seq(...)` | a CRISPR-interference Perturb-seq screen on a gene-regulatory DAG with saturating dynamics, single and double knockdowns, guide escape | **the causal network** (`W`), **noise-free perturbation effects** | 41, 44 |
| `simulate_ld_genotypes(...)` | genotypes with linkage-disequilibrium blocks (a Li–Stephens-style mosaic of ancestral haplotypes) | haplotype structure; used with planted causal SNPs | 35, 44 |
| `simulate_regulatory_sequences(...)`, `regulatory_activity(seq)` | an enhancer reporter assay (MPRA/STARR-seq): DNA sequences with transcription-factor motifs (AP-1, GATA, SP1, E-box, REST) | **the motif grammar** (effects, cooperativity, position, GC), planted sites, a noise-free oracle for variant effects | 36, 42–44 |
| `simulate_helix_bundle(...)` | an idealised four-helix-bundle protein (right-handed α-helices, 3.8 Å Cα spacing) | **3-D coordinates, contacts, secondary structure** | 26–29, 37–39, 43, 44 |
| `simulate_protein_family(...)`, `potts_score`, `deep_mutational_scan(...)` | a protein family (multiple sequence alignment) sampled from a Potts model on the contact map; a deep mutational scan with a non-linear assay | **fields and couplings**, the wild type, **true mutation effects** | 26, 29, 37–39, 43, 44 |
| `simulate_molecules(...)`, `assemble_molecule`, `molecular_fingerprint`, … | a small-molecule library (10 ring scaffolds × substituents, valid SMILES) with potency (pIC50) and solubility assays | **hidden structure–activity rules** and an `oracle` that scores any new design | 28, 39, 40, 42, 44 |

Several Level 2 notebooks add their own small simulators (for example a two-dimensional
"differentiation fork" for diffusion models, a pooled CRISPR fitness screen, a protein family with
structured "chemistry" couplings that small language models can learn, a corpus of synthetic
abstracts for retrieval and agents). They are documented where they are defined.

---

Typed-in examples are kept to a few lines of text each; they are worked examples, not data sets.

## Rules for contributors

- Do not add data files, pictures, downloads or file reads. The validator
  (`python validate_notebooks.py`) rejects stored data files, files over 400 kB, embedded or
  linked pictures (the Colab badge is the only external image), and code that downloads or reads
  data.
- Generate data with the toolkit or with a documented simulation function in the notebook; return
  the hidden truth and use it in a 🧪 ground-truth check.
- Label simulated data (print the `source` line, put "SIMULATED" in plot titles) and explain what
  the simulation mimics and what it cannot teach.
- If a new simulator is useful to several notebooks, add it to `course_toolkit.py`, then rebuild
  every notebook that copies it (the validator reports copies that differ).
